name: MCA territory, temporal
summary: The temporal MCA territory is the lateral temporal lobe supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery: the superior, middle and part of the inferior temporal gyri, the temporal pole, Heschl's gyrus and the planum temporale, with the underlying temporal stem and Meyer's loop of the optic radiation. It is the territory of Wernicke aphasia on the left and of auditory neglect and aprosodia on the right, both with a superior quadrantanopia and no weakness, the pattern of the inferior division stroke that is often mistaken for confusion or psychiatric illness. Its inferior edge with the PCA territory on the inferior temporal gyrus is a watershed.

anatomy.location: Lateral temporal convexity from the temporal pole to the temporo-occipital junction, including the superior and middle temporal gyri, the upper inferior temporal gyrus, the transverse temporal gyri and the planum temporale, and the underlying white matter including the temporal stem and Meyer's loop; bounded above by the Sylvian fissure and the parietal territory, below by the PCA territory and medially by the anterior choroidal territory.

afferents.from: Inferior division of the MCA: anterior, middle and posterior temporal and temporo-occipital arteries

efferents.to: Inferior anastomotic vein of Labbe and the transverse sinus

function: The territory contains the primary and association auditory cortex, the posterior language cortex of the dominant hemisphere, the ventral semantic and auditory identification streams, the temporal pole and the anterior part of the optic radiation, so its infarction produces fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension and repetition on the left, impaired prosody and auditory attention on the right, and a superior quadrantanopia on either side; it is supplied by the anterior, middle and posterior temporal arteries and the temporo-occipital artery of the inferior division, and collateral flow from the PCA along the inferior temporal gyrus limits the infarct in many cases.
